data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"If the underlying storage layer provides atomic append semantics (e.g., a journaling filesystem with fsync, a WAL database, or a distributed log with quorum-based commit), then the clean-halt condition is subsumed by the storage guarantee: either a full event is durably appended or nothing is, regardless of when or why the halt occurs. Under this regime, the distinction between budget halts and crash halts vanishes\u2014both are resumable if the storage layer's atomicity guarantee holds, and resumption must be refused only when the storage guarantee itself is violated (disk failure, corruption, Byzantine storage nodes).","counterconditions":[{"case":"Not all storage layers provide true atomic append: many filesystems allow torn writes (partial sectors) on crash, and fsync may not be honored on all platforms (e.g., ext4 with data=journal vs data=ordered).","eval":"observation"},{"case":"Distributed storage with quorum-based commit may still lose the last event if a minority partition occurs, creating ambiguity about whether the event was committed.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"The atomicity guarantee is at the storage level, but the reasoning system's event may span multiple append operations (e.g., header + body + hash link), each of which is atomic individually but not collectively\u2014requiring a higher-level transaction that reintroduces the partial-write problem.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"Even with atomic storage, if the reasoning system writes the event body before computing and writing the hash link, a crash between these two writes leaves a body without a valid link, which is a different form of partial write.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"SSDs with power-loss protection may silently corrupt pages on unexpected power loss, violating even journaling filesystem guarantees.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The storage layer exposes an atomic append operation: append(event) returns success only after the event is durably persisted and fsync'd, or returns failure if the operation did not complete. The reasoning system calls append for each event and checks the return. Budget exhaustion is checked after append returns\u2014never during. A crash during append leaves either a fully written event or nothing, by the storage layer's guarantee. On resumption, the system reads the log tail and verifies the last event is complete (its declared length matches its actual bytes, and its hash is valid). If so, resumption proceeds; if the storage guarantee was violated (e.g., fsync was not honored, or a partial sector was written), the tail event will fail validation and resumption is refused.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
